collection.description: Behind the gardens, hidden in a tangle of bushes, a villager and some of the other children have built a fort.

ask.text:
Behind the gardens, hidden in a tangle of bushes, (subject) and some of the other children have built a fort. It is made of fallen branches, palm fronds, a great deal of string, and one sleeping mat that nobody will admit to borrowing.
There is a password. Adults are not told the password. Adults who try to guess the password are told, very firmly, that they are wrong, even when they are right.
(adult) strolls past and notices that the fort's roof is sagging alarmingly in the middle, directly over the spot where three children are sitting eating mangoes. How can (adult) help without spoiling the fun?

choices.label: Ask to Hear the Fort's Rules

c1o1.text: (subject) explains the rules with enormous dignity: no grown-ups, no crabs, snacks must be shared, and anyone who knocks the wall down has to fix it. (subject.He/She) is delighted that an adult wanted to know, and as a special honour, (adult) is allowed to sit on the doorstep. Not inside. On the doorstep.

c1o2.text: (subject) starts explaining, then stops, gasps, and announces that (adult) has now heard too much, and the password has to be changed. There is a long consultation inside the fort. The new password turns out to be "banana", which the old password also was. (subject) gives up, laughing, and the fort's secrets remain safe.

c1.text: (adult) stops at a respectful distance outside the fort and asks if (adult.he/she) may please hear the rules. (subject) pokes (subject.his/her) head out, narrows (subject.his/her) eyes, and considers this...

c2o1.text: (adult) shows (subject) how to lash two sticks into a triangle under the sagging middle, and explains why triangles hold their shape better than squares: push a square and it squashes flat, push a triangle and it stays a triangle. (subject) tests this on everything for the rest of the day, and learns a little about why things stand up. The roof holds beautifully.

c2o2.text: After watching (adult) tie one knot, (subject) takes the string firmly. "I can do the rest." So (adult) sits on a nearby stump, ready to leap up if anything falls, and watches (subject) brace the roof alone, slowly, with tongue sticking out in concentration. It holds. Mostly.

c2.text: (adult) mentions, casually, that the roof looks a bit tired, and asks if the fort's builders would like any help. After a whispered meeting, (subject) agrees, "just this once"...

c3o1.text: In the morning, half the fort is lying on the ground. (subject) walks all the way around the wreck, frowning, and then comes running to the builders with a discovery: the walls that were tied to living trees are still standing, and only the loose ones fell over! The builders, who had never thought about it quite that way, start tying the windward sides of their own frames to living trunks.

c3o2.text: In the morning, the whole fort has collapsed into a heap of fronds and string, with the mystery sleeping mat on top. (subject) looks at it for a long time. Then (subject.he/she) picks up a stick and starts drawing in the dirt: a new fort, twice as big, with a tower. "Tomorrow," (subject.he/she) announces to the other children, "we build THIS."

text_only.reason: the word in the owner's story; what changes in the game is the ending's own EFFECT line (the ledger), so this word alone changes nothing

c3.text: (adult) bites (adult.his/her) tongue and says nothing. That night, a strong breeze comes up off the sea and rattles through the gardens...
